newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WHO urges UN to speed medical supplies to Iraq.
newsitem.headline: WHO urges UN to speed medical supplies to Iraq.

text.p: The World Health Organisation said on Wednesday Iraq's health system was near collapse and it urged speedy distribution of medicines and other life-saving supplies due to be imported under the oil-for-food deal.

WHO experts said many of the 1,700 healthcare facilities throughout the country had virtually stopped work, medical supplies were running out and the best and brightest doctors were leaving to seek jobs abroad.

"The situation in Iraq is a total collapse of the health system," said Joseph Hazbun, senior adviser on emergency and humanitarian action who accompanied WHO director-general Hiroshi Nakajima and several experts on a four-day trip to Iraq last month.

Kiyotaka Akasaka, another WHO official, said the United Nations health agency was working with the U.N. Sanctions Committee in New York to speed up its processing of Iraqi contracts with medical suppliers.
"We would like to see the early arrival of supplies," Akasaka said.

The oil-for-food deal, which took effect last December, allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months partly to buy food and medicine for its population of more than 20 million. Iraqis have been suffering under sanctions imposed by the U.N. after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
WHO officials expressed concern that diseases, including malaria, threatened to reappear in large parts of Iraq.
They said hospitals lacked basic medicines and electricity to refrigerate vaccines. Government drug warehouses and pharmacies had few stocks of medicines and medical supplies, they said.
But they had no statistics or independently verified information from the field on the country's health crisis.
"Nobody is reporting anything. Data on Iraq is not reliable. Hospitals don't even have paper to write reports on," Hazbun said.
He said the U.N. Sanctions Committee had approved only one contract out of up to 350 submitted so far.
In most of Iraq, WHO has an observer role to ensure equitable distribution of health products worth $210 million imported into Iraq during the six-month period from December.
WHO is also charged with directly distributing $28.8 million worth of medicines and medical supplies in the three northern governorates where Kurds are under international protection.
WHO plans to employ 20 international staff, backed by 100 local staff, to observe government distribution in most of the country and carry out distribution in the north.
